title: Aitareya Brāhmaṇa
summary: The Brāhmaṇa of the Ṛgvedic hotṛ priests: it explains the recitations of the Soma sacrifice, the Agnihotra and the royal consecration, with the dīkṣā as rebirth of the sacrificer as an embryo (1.3), the legend of Śunaḥśepa recited at the rājasūya (7.13–18), the derivation of the vyāhṛtis and Oṃ from Prajāpati's brooding (5.32), and the rites of kingship and the royal chaplain (book 8).

attribution.tradition: Mahidāsa Aitareya, son of Itarā (Sāyaṇa's introduction; ChU 3.16.7 names Mahidāsa Aitareya)
attribution.scholarly: a compilation of the Aitareyin school of the Ṛgveda; books 1–5 older than 6–8

scholarly.text: c. 800–600 BCE (older books earlier; estimates vary)

structure.description: 8 pañcikās of 5 adhyāyas each (40 adhyāyas), divided into khaṇḍas; cited pañcikā.khaṇḍa

notes: Commentaries: Sāyaṇa; Ṣaḍguruśiṣya (Sukhapradā).

title: Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa
summary: The Brāhmaṇa of the Kauṣītaki (Śāṅkhāyana) school of the Ṛgveda, explaining the fire-establishment, Agnihotra, new- and full-moon, seasonal and Soma rites from the hotṛ's side; it teaches that speech is the consecration and breath the consecrated (7.1) and that speech is spoken most distinctly in the north, where people go to learn it.
notes: The GRETIL e-text numbers the 'speech in the north' passage 7.7 (sentences 35–37); older citations give 7.6.

title: Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa
summary: The Brāhmaṇa of the Taittirīya school of the Black Yajurveda, supplementing the Saṃhitā's own prose: fire establishment, Agnihotra, Soma and royal rites, the nakṣatra offerings, the horse sacrifice, the cosmogony of Prajāpati diving as a boar to raise the earth (1.1.3), and the three Kāṭhaka chapters (3.10–12) on the Sāvitra, Nāciketa and Vaiśvasṛja fire-altars — including Naciketas' visit to Death (3.11.8), Bharadvāja's three lives of Vedic study (3.10.11) and the cosmic session of the world-creators (3.12.9).

attribution.tradition: the Taittirīya school, named after Tittiri (or, in the Purāṇic story, after the partridges (tittiri) who picked up the Yajus disgorged by Yājñavalkya)
attribution.scholarly: compiled within the Taittirīya school; the Kāṭhaka sections (3.10–12) derive from the Kaṭha school

structure.description: 3 aṣṭakas (kāṇḍas) of 8, 8 and 12 prapāṭhakas, divided into anuvākas

notes: Commentaries: Sāyaṇa; Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara.

title: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Mādhyandina)
summary: The 'Brāhmaṇa of a hundred paths', the great Brāhmaṇa of the White Yajurveda. It explains the whole Śrauta ritual — new- and full-moon, fire establishment, Agnihotra, ancestral offering, seasonal rites, Soma, royal consecration, the fire-altar (Agnicayana, books 6–10, with its 'secret' in book 10), horse, human and all-sacrifice, the funeral mound, the Pravargya — and teaches the sacrifice as the cosmic Person and year: Prajāpati fell apart after emitting creatures and is rebuilt in the altar. It records the teaching of Śāṇḍilya (10.6.3), the debates of Yājñavalkya at Janaka's court, the debts, the five great sacrifices, upanayana, Vedic self-study, the flood, and ends with the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (14.4–9).

attribution.tradition: the White Yajus 'from the Sun' proclaimed by Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya (ŚB 14.9.4.33 = BĀU 6.5.3)
attribution.scholarly: a compilation of the Vājasaneyin school; books 6–10 cite Śāṇḍilya as their authority, books 1–5 and 11–14 Yājñavalkya

scholarly.text: c. 8th–6th c. BCE (late Brāhmaṇa period; estimates vary)

structure.description: Mādhyandina recension: 14 kāṇḍas, 100 adhyāyas; cited kāṇḍa.adhyāya.brāhmaṇa.kaṇḍikā

notes: Commentaries: Harisvāmin (partial), Sāyaṇa. See also the Kāṇva recension (src:satapatha-brahmana-kanva).

title: Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Kāṇva recension)
summary: The second recension of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, transmitted by the Kāṇva school of the White Yajurveda; its order of books differs from the Mādhyandina, and its last part is the Kāṇva Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the version on which Śaṅkara commented.
notes: Only partly edited in print for a long time; the Kāṇva BĀU is widely available.

title: Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa
summary: The 'Brāhmaṇa of twenty-five (chapters)' of the Kauthuma–Rāṇāyanīya Sāmaveda: the chants (stotras and stomas) of the Soma sacrifices from one-day rites to year-long sessions, the Vrātya rites (17.1–4) by which outsiders are brought into the sacrificial community, the sessions along the Sarasvatī, and the teaching that Prajāpati alone was, with Speech as his own and his second, and that he released her to pervade all (20.14.2).

scholarly.text: c. 9th–7th c. BCE (among the older Brāhmaṇas; estimate)

notes: Commentary: Sāyaṇa.

title: Ṣaḍviṃśa Brāhmaṇa
summary: The 'twenty-sixth' chapter-book appended to the Pañcaviṃśa: rites of the Sāmaveda not covered there, sorcery and counter-sorcery rites, and in its final part (the Adbhuta Brāhmaṇa) the portents in the world — images of gods that laugh, weep or sweat, strange births and signs in the sky — with the propitiatory rites that avert them.

structure.description: 5 (or 6) prapāṭhakas; the last is the Adbhuta Brāhmaṇa

notes: Commentary: Sāyaṇa. Content of the Adbhuta section given from memory, chapter level.

title: Jaiminīya Brāhmaṇa
summary: The large Brāhmaṇa of the Jaiminīya (Talavakāra) Sāmaveda: an extended treatment of the Agnihotra (1.1–65), the year-long session and Soma rites, and many narratives, including Bhṛgu's journey through the other world where he sees the fruits of deeds (1.42–44) and the fate of the dead questioned at the gate of heaven.
notes: Known from South Indian manuscripts; the Jaiminīya school survives in Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

title: Jaiminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa
summary: The 'secret' Brāhmaṇa of the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda, functioning as that school's Āraṇyaka: meditations on the sāman chant, the udgītha, Oṃ and the breath (prāṇa), the journey of the dead through the sun, and a teacher lineage (vaṃśa); the Kena Upaniṣad forms part of its fourth book.

structure.description: 4 adhyāyas divided into anuvākas and khaṇḍas (numbering differs between editions)

notes: Correction to the task list: it is a Brāhmaṇa (an 'Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa'), not an Āraṇyaka in name, though it plays the Āraṇyaka's role for the Jaiminīyas. The Kena Upaniṣad is usually cited as JUB 4.18–21 (4.10 in Oertel's anuvāka numbering) — locator not verified here.

title: Jaiminīya Ārṣeya Brāhmaṇa
summary: A Jaiminīya Sāmaveda list naming the seers (ṛṣi) of the sāman chants, so that each chant is sung with knowledge of its seer.

title: Sāmavidhāna Brāhmaṇa
summary: A Kauthuma Sāmaveda manual of the application (vidhāna) of sāman chants outside the Soma ritual: expiations, protective and wish-fulfilling rites, and rites for gaining powers, each assigned a chant.

title: Ārṣeya Brāhmaṇa
summary: The Kauthuma Sāmaveda index of the seers (ṛṣi) of the sāman chants; the tradition holds that one who uses a chant without knowing its seer, metre and deity gains no fruit.
notes: Local copy: vedaH/sAma/kauthumam/brAhmaNam (with Sāyaṇa's commentary, OCR).

title: Devatādhyāya Brāhmaṇa
summary: A short Sāmaveda text assigning deities to the sāman chants (and, by some accounts, colours to the metres).

title: Saṃhitopaniṣad Brāhmaṇa
summary: A short Sāmaveda text on the secret meaning of the continuous recitation (saṃhitā) of the chants and on the conditions for their proper transmission.

title: Vaṃśa Brāhmaṇa
summary: A Sāmaveda list of the teachers through whom the Sāmaveda was handed down, traced back through the seers to Kaśyapa, the gods and Prajāpati, and finally to Brahman the self-existent.
notes: Local copy: vedaH/misc/vamsha_brahmana.md.

title: Mantra Brāhmaṇa (Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa)
summary: The Kauthuma Sāmaveda collection of mantras for the domestic rites — marriage, conception, birth and the like — whose continuation (prapāṭhakas 3–10 of the 'Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa') is the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

title: Gopatha Brāhmaṇa
summary: The only surviving Brāhmaṇa of the Atharvaveda. It opens with Brahman, the self-existent, alone in the beginning, who creates a second god from himself (1.1.1), tells of the origin of Atharvan and the Aṅgirases and of the Atharvaveda as the Veda of the brahman priest, discusses Oṃ at length, gives rules for the Vedic student, and in its later part explains Śrauta rites, often in words shared with other Brāhmaṇas.

scholarly.text: late; regarded as later than the major Brāhmaṇas, parts perhaps post-Pāṇinian

title: Kāṭhaka Brāhmaṇa (fragments)
summary: The Brāhmaṇa of the Kaṭha school of the Black Yajurveda, surviving in fragments and in the Kāṭhaka chapters taken into the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (3.10–12) and Āraṇyaka.
notes: Local copy: vedaH/yajur/kaTha/kathaka_brahmana.md.

title: Vādhūla Anvākhyāna (Vādhūla Brāhmaṇa)
summary: Explanatory (Brāhmaṇa-type) narratives of the Vādhūla school of the Black Yajurveda, transmitted with its Śrautasūtra in Kerala manuscripts.
notes: Title and school from memory; content not summarized — gap for Phase C.

title: Śāṭyāyana Brāhmaṇa (lost)
summary: A lost Sāmaveda Brāhmaṇa of the Śāṭyāyanins, known only from quotations (e.g. in Sāyaṇa).

title: Aitareya Āraṇyaka
summary: The 'forest book' of the Aitareyins (Ṛgveda). Book 1 explains the Mahāvrata day; book 2.1–3 teaches the breath (prāṇa) as the recitation (uktha) and as the seers of the Ṛgveda, and the ascending clarity of the self in plants, animals and man (2.3.2); 2.4–6 is the Aitareya Upaniṣad; book 3 (Saṃhitopaniṣad) gives the secret meaning of continuous, word-by-word and step recitation; books 4–5 give the Mahānāmnī verses and the Mahāvrata in sūtra form.

structure.description: 5 āraṇyakas divided into adhyāyas and khaṇḍas

attribution.tradition: books 1–3 Mahidāsa Aitareya; book 4 Āśvalāyana and book 5 Śaunaka (Sāyaṇa)

notes: Commentary: Sāyaṇa; Śaṅkara on the Upaniṣad portion.

title: Kauṣītaki Āraṇyaka (Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka)
summary: The Āraṇyaka of the Kauṣītaki/Śāṅkhāyana Ṛgveda: after chapters on the Mahāvrata it contains the Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad (adhyāyas 3–6, including Pratardana's 'inner Agnihotra', ŚĀ 4.5 = KU 2.5), a Saṃhitopaniṣad on recitation, the contest of the breath with the senses, an interiorized Agnihotra, and a closing teacher lineage.
notes: Order of chapters 7–15 given from memory at chapter level (low confidence).

title: Taittirīya Āraṇyaka
summary: The Āraṇyaka of the Taittirīya Black Yajurveda: the Āruṇaketuka fire-altar (1); the book of Vedic self-study with the twilight worship, the wind-girdled seers who were śramaṇas (2.7) and the five great sacrifices (2.10); the cāturhotra altar (3); the Pravargya mantras and explanation (4–5); the funeral and ancestral mantras (6); the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (7–9); and the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad (10), which contains the mantras of the food-offering into the breaths.

structure.description: 10 prapāṭhakas (Āndhra recension; the Drāviḍa recension differs)

notes: Commentaries: Sāyaṇa; Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara.

title: Kaṭha Āraṇyaka
summary: The Āraṇyaka of the Kaṭha school of the Black Yajurveda, chiefly on the Pravargya rite, recovered from manuscripts.
notes: Local copy: vedaH/yajur/kaTha/kaTha_araNyaka.md.

title: Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad
summary: The tenth prapāṭhaka of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka: a collection of prayers and meditations (to Nārāyaṇa as the supreme, on truth, austerity and renunciation) that includes the mantras spoken when food is offered into the five breaths before a meal.
notes: Owned by U04 (minor Upaniṣads); entered here for the prāṇāgnihotra cross-reference.

title: Prāṇāgnihotra Upaniṣad
summary: A short Upaniṣad of the Muktikā canon (attached to the Atharvaveda) teaching the 'sacrifice in the body' (śārīra-yajña): food eaten with mantras is offered into the breaths as into fires, and the parts and powers of the body and mind are identified with the priests, implements and fires of the sacrifice.
notes: Owned by U04; details of its correspondences not verified — see REPORT.

title: Pāṇinīya Śikṣā
summary: The standard treatise of Vedic phonetics (śikṣā): it counts sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes declared by Svayambhū (v. 3), explains how speech arises when the self, having grasped meanings with the intellect, joins the mind to the wish to speak, the mind strikes the body's fire and the fire impels the breath (vv. 6–9), classifies sounds by place, effort, tone and duration, lists the faults and the virtues of reciters (vv. 32–33), pictures the six Vedāṅgas as the limbs of the Veda (vv. 41–42), warns that a mantra defective in accent or sound harms the sacrificer (v. 52), and ends in homage to Pāṇini, who received the collection of phonemes from Maheśvara (v. 57).

attribution.scholarly: a later compilation in the Pāṇinian school; the text itself speaks of Pāṇini in the third person (vv. 40, 56–57)

structure.description: c. 60 ślokas in the Yajus recension (a shorter Ṛk recension exists)

notes: Local copy: raw_etexts/shixA/sAdhAraNI/paniniya_shiksha.md (verse numbers checked).

title: Yājñavalkya Śikṣā
summary: A phonetic manual of the White Yajurveda (Vājasaneyi) tradition, chiefly on the accents and their marking in recitation.

title: Nāradīya Śikṣā
summary: The Śikṣā of the Sāmaveda: it relates the Vedic accents and the tones of sāman chanting to the seven musical notes (svara) beginning with ṣaḍja, and treats the grāmas, mūrchanās and the manner of singing — a bridge between Vedic phonetics and the later science of music.
notes: Local copy: raw_etexts/shixA/sAma-vedaH/naradiya_shiksha.md. Music theory → U31.

title: Vyāsa Śikṣā
summary: A phonetic manual of the Taittirīya Black Yajurveda, closely related to the Taittirīya Prātiśākhya.

title: Māṇḍūkī Śikṣā
summary: A phonetic manual attached to the Atharvaveda tradition.

title: Vikṛtivallī
summary: A short text on the eight 'modified' recitations (vikṛti) of the Veda — jaṭā, mālā, śikhā, rekhā, dhvaja, daṇḍa, ratha and ghana — by which the text is recited with its words repeated and reversed in fixed patterns so that no syllable can be lost.
notes: Attribution to Vyāḍi and the list of eight from memory — check in Phase C.

title: Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya
summary: The Prātiśākhya of the Śākala Ṛgveda, in verse: the phonemes and their classes, the sandhi rules by which the continuous text (saṃhitā) is formed from Śākalya's word-by-word text (padapāṭha), the step recitation (krama), the accents, and in its last chapters the Vedic metres.

scholarly.text: mid-1st millennium BCE (relative date to Pāṇini disputed)

notes: Commentary: Uvaṭa. Local copy: raw_etexts/shixA/Rg-vedaH/rik_veda_pratishakhya.md.

title: Taittirīya Prātiśākhya
summary: The Prātiśākhya of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (Black Yajurveda): production and classification of sounds, sandhi, accents and the relation of the continuous to the word-by-word text.
notes: Commentaries: Tribhāṣyaratna (Somayārya), Vaidikābharaṇa.

title: Vājasaneyi Prātiśākhya
summary: The Prātiśākhya of the White Yajurveda (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā) in sūtras: phonemes, accents, sandhi and the word-by-word text.
notes: Commentaries: Uvaṭa; Anantabhaṭṭa.

title: Atharvaveda Prātiśākhya (Śaunakīyā Caturādhyāyikā)
summary: The phonetic treatise of the Śaunaka Atharvaveda in four chapters, on sounds, sandhi, accents and the word-by-word text; a second, different Atharvaveda Prātiśākhya is also transmitted.
notes: Local copies: ebhAratI vedAngAni/shixA/atharvavedaprAtishAkhyam(-mUlam).md.

title: Ṛktantra (Sāmaveda Prātiśākhya)
summary: The Prātiśākhya-type phonetic treatise of the Kauthuma–Rāṇāyanīya Sāmaveda.
notes: Attribution varies in the tradition (Śākaṭāyana or Audavraji) — not asserted here.

title: Puṣpasūtra
summary: A Sāmaveda treatise on how the verses are modified into chants — the insertion of stobha syllables, repetitions and other changes by which a ṛk becomes a sāman.

title: Chandaḥśāstra (Chandaḥsūtra) of Piṅgala
summary: The root text of prosody: it defines light and heavy syllables and the eight three-syllable groups (gaṇa) by which metres are described, sets out the Vedic metres (gāyatrī, uṣṇih, anuṣṭubh, bṛhatī, paṅkti, triṣṭubh, jagatī and their varieties) and the classical syllabic and moraic metres, and ends with procedures for enumerating and indexing all possible metrical patterns (prastāra and related operations).

scholarly.text: last centuries BCE (disputed; some place it earlier)

notes: Commentary: Halāyudha's Mṛtasañjīvanī (10th c.). Local copy: Kāvyamālā 91 (OCR). Chapter contents given from memory at chapter level.

title: Nidānasūtra
summary: A Sāmaveda sūtra on the metres of the verses and the structure of the chants and Soma rites.
notes: Sometimes ascribed to a Patañjali; ascription not asserted here.

title: Vṛttaratnākara
summary: Kedārabhaṭṭa's widely studied manual of classical Sanskrit metres, continuing Piṅgala's chandas tradition.
notes: Local copy: gretil 5_poetry/1_chandas.

title: Sarvānukramaṇī
summary: The index of the Ṛgveda hymns giving, for every hymn, its opening words, number of verses, seer (ṛṣi), deity and metre, so that a reciter knows the seer, metre and deity of every mantra he uses.
notes: Commentary: Ṣaḍguruśiṣya's Vedārthadīpikā (12th c.).

title: Bṛhaddevatā
summary: A verse treatise on the deities addressed in the Ṛgveda hymns, with the stories (itihāsa) told to explain them and a discussion of how the deities are ultimately one power in three stations.

title: Ṛgvidhāna
summary: A verse manual of the uses (vidhāna) of Ṛgveda hymns for expiation, protection, healing and the fulfilment of wishes, together with rules of recitation and conduct for the one who uses them.
notes: Local copy: gretil 1_veda/5_vedang/3_pratis/rgvidhana.md.

title: Caraṇavyūha
summary: A short supplement (pariśiṣṭa) listing the branches (śākhā) of the four Vedas and the auxiliary sciences, including the four Upavedas — medicine (āyurveda), archery/warfare (dhanurveda), music (gāndharvaveda) and statecraft/architecture — attached to the four Vedas.
notes: The assignment of the fourth Upaveda (arthaśāstra or sthāpatyaveda) varies between sources; attribution (Śaunaka?) not asserted.

title: Atharvaveda Pariśiṣṭas
summary: About seventy supplementary texts of the Atharvaveda on royal rites, omens and portents, astral lore, rites of appeasement (śānti), gifts, and the duties of the royal chaplain.
notes: Local copy: gretil 1_veda/5_vedang/2_paris/atharvavedaparisistas.md.

title: Aṣṭādhyāyī
summary: Pāṇini's grammar of Sanskrit in 'eight chapters': nearly four thousand ordered rules (sūtra) that derive every correct word of the spoken language (bhāṣā) and of the Veda (chandas) from roots, stems and affixes by means of technical terms, metarules and abbreviations (pratyāhāra) built on the fourteen Māheśvara sūtras. It defines, among much else, the agent as 'the independent one' (1.4.54), the three accents (1.2.29–31) and the three vowel quantities (1.2.27), and it names ten earlier grammarians.

attribution.tradition: Pāṇini, who received the phoneme list from Śiva (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 56–57; Nandikeśvara)

structure.description: 8 adhyāyas × 4 pādas; nearly 4,000 sūtras; with the Dhātupāṭha, Gaṇapāṭha, Uṇādisūtras and Liṅgānuśāsana as auxiliary lists

notes: Its philosophy-of-language reception (Bhartṛhari, sphoṭa) belongs to U31 / lin:vyakarana.

title: Māheśvara Sūtras (Śivasūtras of the grammarians)
summary: The fourteen short lists of phonemes (a i u ṇ, ṛ ḷ k, … ha l) prefixed to the Aṣṭādhyāyī, from which Pāṇini forms his abbreviations (pratyāhāra) of sound-classes; by tradition they were the fourteen beats of Śiva's drum at the end of his dance.
notes: Not to be confused with Vasugupta's Śiva Sūtra (src:siva-sutra, Kashmir Śaivism).

title: Nandikeśvara-kāśikā
summary: A short verse commentary ascribed to Nandikeśvara that reads the fourteen Māheśvara sūtras as teachings on the supreme reality and its manifestation; it opens with the story that at the end of his dance Śiva, the king of dancers, sounded his drum fourteen times to uplift Sanaka and the other perfected sages.
notes: Date and verse numbers not verified; the opening story is widely quoted.

title: Dhātupāṭha (Pāṇinīya)
summary: The list of verbal roots used by the Aṣṭādhyāyī, arranged in ten classes (gaṇa) with markers and glosses of meaning.
notes: The meaning-glosses are generally held to be later additions.

title: Gaṇapāṭha
summary: The lists of words (gaṇa) referred to in the Aṣṭādhyāyī by their first member ('sarva and the rest' and so on).

title: Uṇādisūtra
summary: The sūtras deriving nouns with the 'uṇ and following' affixes from verbal roots — the grammarians' practical carrying-out of the thesis that nouns come from verbs.
notes: Ascribed by some to Śākaṭāyana, by others to Pāṇini or later authors; not asserted here.

title: Vārttikas of Kātyāyana
summary: Kātyāyana's critical remarks (vārttika) on Pāṇini's rules — supplements, restrictions and corrections — preserved within Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya. The first vārttika declares that word, meaning and their relation are established (siddha) and that grammar restricts usage for the sake of dharma.

structure.description: several thousand vārttikas on a part of Pāṇini's sūtras (count varies by reckoning)

title: Vyākaraṇa-Mahābhāṣya
summary: Patañjali's 'great commentary' on Pāṇini's sūtras and Kātyāyana's vārttikas, in lively dialogue. Its introduction (Paspaśā) asks what a word is, gives the purposes of studying grammar — protection of the Veda, adaptation of mantras, the scriptural command, brevity and certainty — tells how Bṛhaspati taught Indra words one by one for a thousand divine years without reaching the end, reads the Ṛgveda's 'four horns' verse as a praise of grammar, and holds that the Asuras were defeated for mispronouncing speech.

scholarly.text: c. mid-2nd c. BCE (the text refers to sacrificing for Puṣyamitra)

structure.description: 85 āhnikas ('daily lessons'), the first being the Paspaśā

editions.name: Kielhorn's edition via GRETIL (local Devanāgarī mirror)

title: Kāśikāvṛtti
summary: The first complete running commentary on the Aṣṭādhyāyī, rule by rule, with examples; the standard entry to Pāṇini before the Kaumudī works.

title: Nyāsa (Kāśikāvivaraṇapañjikā)
summary: Jinendrabuddhi's sub-commentary on the Kāśikāvṛtti.

title: Padamañjarī
summary: Haradatta's sub-commentary on the Kāśikāvṛtti.
notes: Whether this Haradatta is the Dharmasūtra commentator of the same name is uncertain.

title: Mahābhāṣya-pradīpa
summary: Kaiyaṭa's commentary on Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya, the basis of later Pāṇinian scholarship.

title: Vaiyākaraṇa-Siddhāntakaumudī
summary: Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita's rearrangement of Pāṇini's rules by topic and by the order of derivation (prakriyā), the standard textbook of traditional grammar.

title: Laghusiddhāntakaumudī
summary: Varadarāja's abridgement of the Siddhāntakaumudī for beginners.

title: Prakriyākaumudī
summary: Rāmacandra's derivation-ordered treatment of Pāṇinian grammar, a forerunner of the Siddhāntakaumudī.

title: Paribhāṣenduśekhara
summary: Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa's treatise on the interpretive metarules (paribhāṣā) by which Pāṇini's sūtras are applied.

title: Kātantra (Kalāpa)
summary: A concise non-Pāṇinian grammar attributed to Śarvavarman, organized for quick learning; widely used in Bengal, Kashmir and in Tibet.

attribution.tradition: composed by Śarvavarman to teach a Sātavāhana king Sanskrit quickly

title: Cāndra-vyākaraṇa
summary: Candragomin's grammar, closely based on Pāṇini but without Vedic rules and accents, transmitted especially in Buddhist circles (Nepal, Tibet, Sri Lanka).

title: Jainendra-vyākaraṇa
summary: Pūjyapāda Devanandin's Pāṇini-based grammar for Jain use.

title: Śākaṭāyana Śabdānuśāsana (of Pālyakīrti)
summary: A grammar by the Yāpanīya Jain Pālyakīrti, who took the name of the ancient grammarian Śākaṭāyana; not the lost work of the Śākaṭāyana cited by Yāska and Pāṇini.

title: Siddhahemaśabdānuśāsana
summary: Hemacandra's grammar of Sanskrit and (in its eighth chapter) of the Prakrits and Apabhraṃśa.

title: Mugdhabodha
summary: Bopadeva's short non-Pāṇinian grammar, much used in Bengal.

title: Prākṛtaprakāśa
summary: The oldest surviving grammar of the Prakrits (Mahārāṣṭrī, Paiśācī, Māgadhī, Śaurasenī), ascribed to Vararuci.

attribution.tradition: Vararuci, whom tradition identifies with Kātyāyana
attribution.scholarly: a Vararuci of uncertain date; commentary by Bhāmaha

title: Nighaṇṭu
summary: The traditional word-list (samāmnāya) on which the Nirukta comments: three chapters of synonyms (names of earth, water, speech, and so on), one of single difficult Vedic words, and one of the names of the deities by region.

attribution.tradition: handed down (samāmnāta) from the seers; some later authorities ascribe it to Yāska

title: Nirukta
summary: Yāska's explanation of the Nighaṇṭu and of Vedic words. Book 1 sets out the four classes of words (1.1), Vārṣyāyaṇi's six modifications of being (1.2), the dispute whether all nouns come from verbs (1.12–14), Kautsa's claim that mantras are meaningless and its refutation (1.15–16), praise of understanding (1.18) and the origin of the Veda and Vedāṅgas from the seers' direct vision (1.20); book 2 gives the rules of etymology (2.1) and of teaching (2.3–4) and defines the seer as the one who saw (2.11); books 7–12 explain the deities as three, of one self praised in many ways (7.4–5).

scholarly.text: generally held to precede Pāṇini (mid-1st millennium BCE); exact date uncertain

title: Durgavṛtti on the Nirukta
summary: Durga's commentary on Yāska's Nirukta.

title: Nirukta-bhāṣya-ṭīkā of Skandasvāmin and Maheśvara
summary: A commentary on the Nirukta begun by Skandasvāmin and continued by Maheśvara.

title: Nighaṇṭu-nirvacana of Devarāja Yajvan
summary: Devarāja Yajvan's commentary on the Nighaṇṭu.

title: Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa
summary: Lagadha's manual of Vedic time-reckoning for fixing the times of sacrifices: a five-year cycle (yuga) of lunar and solar time presided over by Prajāpati, the twenty-seven lunar mansions (nakṣatra), the lunar days, the solstices (the northward turning of sun and moon at the beginning of Śraviṣṭhā), and rules for intercalation. It declares that the Vedas exist for the sacrifices, the sacrifices depend on time, and so this science of time stands at the head of the Vedāṅgas.

attribution.tradition: the teaching of Lagadha, the great-souled (v. 2)
attribution.scholarly: Lagadha, known only from this text

scholarly.text: composition usually placed in the second half of the 1st millennium BCE; the solstitial position it states has been dated by some to the 2nd millennium BCE (disputed)

structure.description: Ārca (Ṛgveda) recension of 36 verses and Yājuṣa recension of 43–44 verses

notes: Commentary on the Yājuṣa recension: Somākara. Later jyotiṣa → U32.

title: Ātharvaṇa Jyotiṣa
summary: A later Atharvaveda text on auspicious timing: the lunar mansions, lunar days, divisions of the day and their suitability for actions.

title: Āpastamba Kalpasūtra
summary: The complete ritual corpus of the Āpastamba branch of the Taittirīya Black Yajurveda: Śrautasūtra, a Mantrapāṭha for the domestic rites, Gṛhyasūtra, Dharmasūtra and Śulbasūtra, transmitted as one work in thirty praśnas.

structure.description: 30 praśnas: 1–24 Śrauta (24 includes the paribhāṣās), 25–26 Mantrapāṭha, 27 Gṛhya, 28–29 Dharma, 30 Śulba

notes: Praśna division from memory; the grouping into four sūtras is certain.

title: Baudhāyana Kalpasūtra
summary: The complete ritual corpus of the Baudhāyana branch of the Taittirīya school — Śrauta, Karmānta, Dvaidha, Gṛhya, Dharma and Śulba sūtras — regarded as the oldest of the sūtra corpora, written in a discursive, Brāhmaṇa-like prose.

title: Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra
summary: The Śrauta manual of the Ṛgvedic hotṛ priest (Śākala/Āśvalāyana school), 12 adhyāyas, setting out the recitations for the new- and full-moon, seasonal and Soma rites.

title: Śāṅkhāyana Śrautasūtra
summary: The Śrauta manual of the Kauṣītaki/Śāṅkhāyana Ṛgveda, in 18 adhyāyas, including the Mahāvrata and long sessions.

title: Kātyāyana Śrautasūtra
summary: The Śrauta manual of the White Yajurveda, following the order of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, in 26 adhyāyas; its opening sets out who is qualified to sacrifice.

title: Baudhāyana Śrautasūtra
summary: The oldest Śrautasūtra of the Taittirīya school, discursive in style and close to the Brāhmaṇas.

title: Āpastamba Śrautasūtra
summary: The Śrauta manual of the Āpastamba Taittirīyas (praśnas 1–24 of the Kalpasūtra); its general rules define the Veda as mantra and brāhmaṇa (24.1.31) and the Brāhmaṇa as injunctions to action.

title: Bhāradvāja Śrautasūtra
summary: The Śrauta manual of the Bhāradvāja branch of the Taittirīya school.

title: Hiraṇyakeśi (Satyāṣāḍha) Śrautasūtra
summary: The Śrauta manual of the Hiraṇyakeśin branch of the Taittirīya school, part of a complete Kalpasūtra ascribed to Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin.

title: Vaikhānasa Śrautasūtra
summary: The Śrauta manual of the Vaikhānasa branch of the Taittirīya school.

title: Vādhūla Śrautasūtra
summary: The Śrauta manual of the Vādhūla school of the Black Yajurveda, preserved in Kerala.

title: Mānava Śrautasūtra
summary: The Śrauta manual of the Mānava branch of the Maitrāyaṇīya Black Yajurveda.

title: Vārāha Śrautasūtra
summary: The Śrauta manual of the Vārāha branch of the Maitrāyaṇīya Black Yajurveda.

title: Lāṭyāyana Śrautasūtra
summary: The Śrauta manual of the Kauthuma Sāmaveda singers (udgātṛ).

title: Drāhyāyaṇa Śrautasūtra
summary: The Śrauta manual of the Rāṇāyanīya Sāmaveda singers.

title: Jaiminīya Śrautasūtra
summary: The Śrauta manual of the Jaiminīya Sāmaveda.

title: Maśaka Kalpasūtra (Ārṣeya Kalpa)
summary: A Sāmaveda sūtra listing the chants used in each Soma rite.

title: Vaitāna Sūtra
summary: The Śrauta manual of the Atharvaveda, chiefly for the brahman priest's part in the solemn rites.

title: Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the Āśvalāyana Ṛgvedins in 4 adhyāyas: the three kinds of cooked offering (1.1.2), marriage — for which the customs of regions and villages are to be followed (1.7.1) — pregnancy and birth rites, initiation at eight, eleven or twelve (1.19), the Vedic student's vows, and in book 4 the treatment of the dying āhitāgni, cremation, collecting the bones and the ancestral rites.

structure.description: 4 adhyāyas divided into khaṇḍas and sūtras

title: Śāṅkhāyana Gṛhyasūtra
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the Śāṅkhāyana Ṛgvedins.

title: Kauṣītaka Gṛhyasūtra
summary: A domestic-rite manual of the Kauṣītaki Ṛgvedins.

title: Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtra
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the White Yajurveda (also called Kātīya or Vājasaneyi Gṛhyasūtra), in 3 kāṇḍas, much used in North India for marriage (with the seven steps), initiation and funeral water-offerings.

title: Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the Āpastamba Taittirīyas (praśna 27 of the Kalpasūtra), used with its Mantrapāṭha.

title: Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the Baudhāyana Taittirīyas, with supplementary sections (pariśiṣṭa, śeṣa sūtras).

title: Bhāradvāja Gṛhyasūtra
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the Bhāradvāja Taittirīyas.

title: Hiraṇyakeśi Gṛhyasūtra
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the Hiraṇyakeśin Taittirīyas.

title: Vaikhānasa Gṛhyasūtra (Smārtasūtra)
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the Vaikhānasas, including the eighteen bodily rites and the domestic worship of Viṣṇu.

title: Mānava Gṛhyasūtra
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the Mānava Maitrāyaṇīyas.

title: Vārāha Gṛhyasūtra
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the Vārāha Maitrāyaṇīyas.

title: Kāṭhaka Gṛhyasūtra (Laugākṣi)
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the Kaṭha school, ascribed to Laugākṣi.

title: Vādhūla Gṛhyasūtra
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the Vādhūla school.

title: Gobhila Gṛhyasūtra
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the Kauthuma Sāmavedins, used with the Mantra Brāhmaṇa.

title: Khādira Gṛhyasūtra
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the Rāṇāyanīya (Drāhyāyaṇa) Sāmavedins, an abridgement close to Gobhila.

title: Jaiminīya Gṛhyasūtra
summary: The domestic-rite manual of the Jaiminīya Sāmavedins.

title: Kauśika Sūtra
summary: The domestic and magical rite manual of the Śaunaka Atharvaveda: healing rites with the Atharvan hymns, rites for prosperity, protection and against enemies, marriage, funeral and ancestral rites.

title: Karmapradīpa (Gobhila-smṛti)
summary: A verse supplement to the Sāmavedic domestic rites (Chāndogya pariśiṣṭa), on sacred thread, sipping, the daily offerings, śrāddha and impurity.

title: Baudhāyana Śulbasūtra
summary: The oldest 'cord-rules': how to lay out with cord and pegs the sacrificial grounds, fire-altars and bricks of prescribed shapes and areas — squares, rectangles, the falcon-shaped altar and its enlargements — including the rule relating the diagonal of a rectangle to its sides, and transformations of one figure into another of equal area.
notes: Described only as what the text teaches for ritual construction; no modern mathematical interpretation is added here.

title: Āpastamba Śulbasūtra
summary: The Āpastamba rules for measuring and constructing the altars (praśna 30 of the Kalpasūtra).

title: Kātyāyana Śulbasūtra
summary: The White Yajurveda rules for measuring and constructing the altars.

title: Mānava Śulbasūtra
summary: The Maitrāyaṇīya (Mānava) altar-construction rules.

title: Maitrāyaṇīya Śulbasūtra
summary: A Maitrāyaṇīya altar-construction text transmitted separately from the Mānava.

title: Āpastamba Dharmasūtra
summary: The Dharmasūtra of the Āpastamba Kalpasūtra (praśnas 28–29). It grounds dharma in the agreement of those who know it and in the Vedas (1.1.1.2–3), sets out the four classes and the student's life, contains a chapter on the attainment of the self and the removal of the faults that burn beings through yoga (1.8.22–23), treats the householder, inheritance and the king, lists four orders of life while criticizing the renouncer's claim of liberation by knowledge alone (2.9.21–24), teaches that the classes rise or fall in the next birth by conduct (2.5.11.10–11), and ends that the rest of dharma should be learned from women and from all classes (2.11.29.15).

scholarly.text: c. 3rd c. BCE (recent estimate; older estimates c. 450–350 BCE)

structure.description: 2 praśnas, divided into paṭalas, khaṇḍas and sūtras (cited here praśna.paṭala.khaṇḍa.sūtra)

notes: Commentary: Haradatta's Ujjvalā.

title: Gautama Dharmasūtra
summary: A Dharmasūtra not attached to a surviving Kalpasūtra (associated with the Sāmaveda). It opens 'the Veda is the root of dharma' (1.1), reports that some allow a choice among the life-orders while 'the teachers' hold there is only one, the householder's, because only it is directly enjoined in the Veda (3.1, 3.36), lists the forty sacraments and the eight virtues of the self and declares that the virtues, not the sacraments alone, lead to Brahman (8.14–25), makes regional, caste and family customs authoritative where not contrary to the Veda (11.20), and gives the means of expiation (19.11–12).

scholarly.text: c. 2nd c. BCE (recent estimate; older estimates c. 600–400 BCE)

structure.description: 28 adhyāyas of sūtras (cited in Stenzler's numbering, as in the GRETIL e-text)

notes: Commentaries: Maskarin; Haradatta's Mitākṣarā.

title: Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra
summary: The Dharmasūtra of the Baudhāyana Kalpasūtra (with later books). It defines the cultured (śiṣṭa) whose practice is authoritative (1.1.1.5–6), records the five practices peculiar to the south and the north and Gautama's rejection of them (1.1.2.1–8), sets out the four orders and the teachers' view that there is only one, telling that the divisions were made by the asura Kapila, son of Prahlāda, in rivalry with the gods (2.6.11.27–28), and treats expiations, the householder's livelihoods, the forest-dweller and the renouncer.

scholarly.text: core c. 2nd c. BCE, later books added

structure.description: 4 praśnas (the last parts later), cited praśna.adhyāya.khaṇḍa.sūtra as in the GRETIL e-text

notes: Commentary: Govindasvāmin.

title: Vasiṣṭha Dharmasūtra
summary: A Dharmasūtra associated with the Ṛgveda. It places dharma in śruti and smṛti and, failing these, in the practice of the cultured, 'one free of desire' (1.4–6); teaches that the Vedas do not purify one without right conduct, and leave him at death as fledglings leave the nest (6.3); lets a student who has kept his vow enter whichever order he wishes (7.1–3); tells the renouncer to give up all rites but never the Veda (10.4); and ends: 'practise dharma, not adharma; speak truth, not untruth; look far, not near; look to the highest, not to what is not highest' (30.1).

title: Vaikhānasa Dharmasūtra
summary: The Dharma portion of the Vaikhānasa Smārtasūtra: the four orders with detailed classes of householders, forest-dwellers and renouncers, their livelihoods and disciplines.

title: Hiraṇyakeśi Dharmasūtra
summary: The Dharmasūtra of the Hiraṇyakeśin Kalpasūtra, largely taken over from Āpastamba.

title: Manusmṛti (Mānava Dharmaśāstra)
summary: The most authoritative metrical code of dharma, spoken by Bhṛgu on behalf of Manu Svāyambhuva. Book 1 tells of creation from the self-existent, the four classes from the mouth, arms, thighs and feet (1.31), the Manus, the ages and their declining dharma (1.68–86); book 2 the sources of dharma (2.6, 2.12), the sacraments, the syllable Oṃ, the Sāvitrī and recitation (2.76–87), control of the senses and the student's life with the teacher; book 3 marriage, the five great sacrifices and the ancestral rites; book 4 the householder and the snātaka; book 5 food, death-impurity and purification, and women; book 6 the forest-dweller and the renouncer, breath control and meditation, and the tenfold dharma; books 7–9 kingship and law; book 10 the classes and mixed castes and dharma in distress; book 11 gifts and expiation; book 12 the fruits of action, the three guṇas, rebirth, the highest good and the vision of the self in all beings.

attribution.tradition: taught by Manu Svāyambhuva, who received it from Svayambhū, and recited to the seers by Bhṛgu (1.58–60); Nārada's preface tells of an original of 100,000 verses successively abridged
attribution.scholarly: a single composition or redaction by an unknown brāhmaṇa author (or school) drawing on the Dharmasūtras

tradition.text: from the beginning of creation (the first Manu's teaching)

scholarly.text: c. 2nd c. BCE – 2nd c. CE (one recent estimate: 2nd c. CE)

structure.description: 12 adhyāyas, c. 2,700 ślokas (verse numbers cited in Kullūka's vulgate numbering as in the GRETIL e-text)

editions.name: GRETIL e-text (Yano & Ikari; Kullūka base with Medhātithi variants), local mirror

notes: Commentaries: Medhātithi, Govindarāja, Kullūka, Nārāyaṇa, Rāghavānanda, Nandana and others.

title: Yājñavalkyasmṛti
summary: A concise metrical code taught by the sage Yājñavalkya in Mithilā, in three books: conduct (ācāra) — sources of dharma, the fourteen branches of knowledge and the twenty lawgivers (1.3–5), the highest dharma as seeing the self through yoga (1.8), the sacraments, twilight worship with breath control (1.22–25), the householder, śrāddha and kingship; legal procedure (vyavahāra) — where dharmaśāstra prevails over arthaśāstra (2.21); and expiation (prāyaścitta) — death-impurity and funeral rites (3.1ff), the renouncer, and an extended teaching on the self, its embodiment, meditation, the self as one and many like space in pots (3.144), liberation through music for one who knows the vīṇā (3.115), and the signs of yogic power (3.202–203).

attribution.tradition: the Vedic sage Yājñavalkya, 'lord of yogins', teaching in Mithilā (1.1–2)
attribution.scholarly: a later composition bearing his name, drawing on Manu

notes: Commentaries: Viśvarūpa (Bālakrīḍā), Vijñāneśvara (Mitākṣarā), Aparārka, Śūlapāṇi (Dīpakalikā).

title: Nāradasmṛti
summary: The first Dharmaśāstra devoted wholly to law and legal procedure (vyavahāra): its introduction teaches that when people were devoted to dharma and truthful there was no litigation, and that legal procedure arose when dharma was lost among humans (Mātṛkā 1.1–2); it then treats the eighteen titles of law.
notes: Commentary: Asahāya (revised by Kalyāṇabhaṭṭa). Numbering 'm1' = Mātṛkā 1 as in the GRETIL e-text.

title: Viṣṇusmṛti (Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra)
summary: A Dharmaśāstra framed as Viṣṇu's teaching to the Earth goddess, in mixed prose and verse (100 chapters), covering the classes and orders, law, impurity, śrāddha and holy places for it, vows and fasts, expiation, the duties of women (including the widow's choice of chastity or ascending the pyre, 25.14), and devotion and meditation on Vāsudeva.

attribution.tradition: taught by Viṣṇu (in his boar form, to the Earth)
attribution.scholarly: a Vaiṣṇava recasting of an older Dharmasūtra

scholarly.text: c. 7th c. CE in its present form (with an older core)

notes: Commentary: Nandapaṇḍita's Vaijayantī.

title: Parāśarasmṛti
summary: The smṛti declared authoritative for the Kali age: the seers ask Vyāsa for the dharma of the present age and are led to Parāśara, who teaches that Manu's dharma belongs to the Kṛta age, Gautama's to the Tretā, Śaṅkha and Likhita's to the Dvāpara and Parāśara's to the Kali (1.24), and sets out conduct and a lenient system of expiation.
notes: Commentary: Mādhava's Parāśaramādhavīya.

title: Bṛhaspatismṛti
summary: A lost legal smṛti, reconstructed from quotations in the digests; its treatment of legal procedure and the titles of law was highly regarded.

title: Kātyāyanasmṛti
summary: A lost legal smṛti on procedure and the titles of law, reconstructed from quotations.

title: Hārīta Dharmasūtra / Hārītasmṛti (fragments)
summary: An old Dharma text of Hārīta, lost and known from quotations (later metrical Laghu- and Vṛddha-Hārīta texts exist); it is often cited for the distinction between women who are 'speakers of Brahman' (brahmavādinī) and those who marry directly (sadyovadhū).
notes: The brahmavādinī/sadyovadhū quotation is known through later digests; wording not verified here.

title: Śaṅkha-Likhita Dharmasūtra (fragments)
summary: A lost Dharmasūtra of the brothers Śaṅkha and Likhita, named by Parāśara as the authority of the Dvāpara age; known from quotations.

title: Devalasmṛti
summary: A smṛti ascribed to Devala, quoted in the digests (also on Sāṃkhya-yoga); a short text by this name survives.

title: Vyāsasmṛti
summary: A short metrical smṛti ascribed to Vyāsa on the classes, sacraments, the householder and daily duties.

title: Dakṣasmṛti
summary: A short metrical smṛti on the orders of life, the householder's daily routine, purity and yoga.

title: Āṅgirasasmṛti
summary: A short smṛti ascribed to Aṅgiras, chiefly on expiation.
notes: Local copy: gretil 4_dharma/smrti/angirasasmrti.

title: Yamasmṛti
summary: Short smṛtis ascribed to Yama (several versions of 78, 99 and 182 verses and a South Indian recension), chiefly on expiation and impurity.
notes: Local copies: gretil 4_dharma/smrti/yamasmrti*, brhadyamasmrti, laghuyamasmrti.

title: Atrismṛti
summary: A short smṛti ascribed to Atri, one of the twenty lawgivers named by Yājñavalkya (1.4–5).
notes: Contents not summarized here — gap.

title: Saṃvartasmṛti
summary: A short smṛti ascribed to Saṃvarta, one of the twenty lawgivers of Yājñavalkya 1.4–5.
notes: Contents not summarized here — gap.

title: Uśanasmṛti
summary: A short smṛti ascribed to Uśanas, one of the twenty lawgivers of Yājñavalkya 1.4–5.
notes: Contents not summarized here — gap.

title: Śātātapasmṛti
summary: A short smṛti ascribed to Śātātapa, one of the twenty lawgivers, chiefly on expiation.

title: Manubhāṣya of Medhātithi
summary: The oldest surviving commentary on Manu, applying Mīmāṃsā reasoning to its verses; it argues, among much else, against the widow's following her husband in death.

title: Manvarthamuktāvalī of Kullūka
summary: Kullūka Bhaṭṭa's concise commentary on Manu, the basis of the vulgate text and numbering.

title: Bālakrīḍā of Viśvarūpa
summary: The oldest surviving commentary on the Yājñavalkyasmṛti.

title: Mitākṣarā of Vijñāneśvara
summary: Vijñāneśvara's commentary on the Yājñavalkyasmṛti, written at the Cālukya court of Kalyāṇa; the most influential work of Dharmaśāstra, founding the view that sons own ancestral property by birth and that kinship (sapiṇḍa) rests on shared bodily particles.

title: Aparārka's commentary on Yājñavalkya
summary: The extensive commentary on the Yājñavalkyasmṛti by the Śilāhāra king Aparāditya (Aparārka), rich in quotations from lost smṛtis.

title: Ujjvalā of Haradatta
summary: Haradatta's commentary on the Āpastamba Dharmasūtra.

title: Maskari-bhāṣya on Gautama
summary: Maskarin's commentary on the Gautama Dharmasūtra.

title: Govindasvāmin's commentary on Baudhāyana
summary: Govindasvāmin's commentary on the Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra.

title: Vaijayantī of Nandapaṇḍita
summary: Nandapaṇḍita's commentary on the Viṣṇusmṛti.

title: Dāyabhāga of Jīmūtavāhana
summary: The Bengal treatise on inheritance and partition, arguing against the Mitākṣarā that heirs acquire ownership only on the owner's death and that heirship follows the capacity to benefit the dead by ancestral offerings.

title: Kṛtyakalpataru of Lakṣmīdhara
summary: The earliest great digest (nibandha), in fourteen books arranging smṛti quotations by topic: the student, householder, daily rites, śrāddha, gifts, pilgrimage, vows, purification, kingship, law, liberation (mokṣa) and others.

title: Smṛticandrikā of Devaṇṇabhaṭṭa
summary: A South Indian digest of Dharmaśāstra on conduct, law and impurity.

title: Caturvargacintāmaṇi of Hemādri
summary: Hemādri's vast digest on the four aims of life, of which the parts on vows (vrata), gifts (dāna), pilgrimage, śrāddha and the division of time survive.

title: Parāśaramādhavīya
summary: Mādhava's large commentary-digest on the Parāśarasmṛti, the standard South Indian authority on conduct and expiation for the Kali age.

attribution.tradition: Mādhavācārya, whom tradition identifies with Vidyāraṇya after renunciation
attribution.scholarly: Mādhava of the Vijayanagara court (14th c.); the identification with Vidyāraṇya is debated

title: Kālanirṇaya of Mādhava
summary: Mādhava's treatise on the proper times of rites, fasts and festivals.

title: Smṛtitattva of Raghunandana
summary: Raghunandana's series of twenty-eight 'essences' (tattva) on ritual, time, impurity, śrāddha, inheritance and expiation, the authority for Bengal.

title: Nirṇayasindhu of Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa
summary: Kamalākara Bhaṭṭa's digest deciding the correct times and procedures of rites, fasts, festivals, sacraments and śrāddha.
notes: Local copies: raw_etexts/kalpaH/nirNaya-sindhuH (OCR).

title: Bhagavantabhāskara of Nīlakaṇṭha Bhaṭṭa
summary: Nīlakaṇṭha Bhaṭṭa's digest in twelve 'rays' (mayūkha) — on sacraments, conduct, time, śrāddha, law (Vyavahāramayūkha), expiation and others.

title: Vīramitrodaya of Mitra Miśra
summary: Mitra Miśra's encyclopaedic digest in many 'illuminations' (prakāśa) — on sacraments, conduct, time, pilgrimage, śrāddha, law, expiation and liberation.

title: Dharmasindhu of Kāśīnātha Upādhyāya
summary: A late comprehensive manual of the times and rules of rites, vows, sacraments, śrāddha and impurity, widely followed in western India.
notes: Local copy: ebhAratI dharmasUtrANi/dharmasindhuH.md. Author entered only in attribution text.

title: Antyeṣṭi-paddhatis (funeral manuals)
summary: The family of practical manuals (paddhati) for the funeral rites — preparing the dying, cremation, collecting the bones, water-offerings, the first-year offerings and the uniting of the dead with the ancestors — composed for each Vedic school.
notes: Collective entry for a genre; individual titles not listed (gap).

title: Kauṭilīya Arthaśāstra
summary: The science of statecraft: the training and conduct of the king, administration, law and punishment, foreign policy and war. It names the four sciences — investigation (Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Lokāyata), the triple Veda, economics and governance — calling investigation 'the lamp of all sciences' (1.2.1–12); gives the duties common to all (non-injury, truth, purity, freedom from envy, compassion, patience) and says one's own dharma leads to heaven and infinity (1.3.13–14); and holds that artha is foremost among the three aims because dharma and kāma are rooted in it (1.7.6–7).

attribution.tradition: Kauṭilya (Cāṇakya, Viṣṇugupta), minister of Candragupta Maurya
attribution.scholarly: a composite work redacted in the early centuries CE on older sources

scholarly.text: redaction c. 1st–3rd c. CE on sources from c. 2nd c. BCE

title: Kāmasūtra of Vātsyāyana
summary: The śāstra of the third aim. Its second chapter teaches that a man with a span of a hundred years should divide his time and pursue the three aims so that they support and do not harm one another — learning and wealth in youth, love in early manhood, dharma and liberation in old age (1.2.1–4) — that of the three each earlier is weightier (1.2.14), and answers objections of Mīmāṃsakas and of Lokāyatikas, who say dharma's fruit is future and doubtful: 'better a pigeon today than a peacock tomorrow' (1.2.21–24).
notes: Only the trivarga teaching is recorded here; the text's other contents are out of scope. Commentary: Yaśodhara's Jayamaṅgalā.
